newsitem.title: UK: Dlr calm in Europe as traders digest volatile week.
newsitem.headline: Dlr calm in Europe as traders digest volatile week.

text.p: The dollar was trading slightly firmer against the mark and yen early in Europe as markets stabilised following a volatile week of sharp yen gains and shifting interest rate expectations in Japan and the U.S.

Traders in Tokyo said the overnight session was dominated by short-covering on this week's steep decline in dollar/yen but the recovery was limited and capped at 117 yen. Dollar/mark continued to outperform and held firm above 1.70 in Europe.
"Things are calmer and people seem to be digesting what was a very eventful week. We're starting to focus now on the FOMC next week," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.

"The big question now is whether the U.S. economy has slowed enough to prevent the Fed from tightening and on balance we think they will leave rates unchanged next week," said Knuthsen. "The market has scaled back its expectations and if they do raise rates the dollar could get a boost."
The Federal Reserve's policy-making Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday.

At 0800 GMT, the dollar was trading at 116.25/35 yen, little changed from 116.20/25 late on Thursday but well off the overnight high at 117.00. Against the mark, it was at 1.7010/15, compared with 1.6990/00 late yesterday as the mark/yen cross stayed soft.
The dollar/yen has collapsed from 4-1/2-year highs this month and lost almost 10 percent of its value in just two weeks.

The reversal was triggered by a barrage of verbal intervention from Japanese officials aimed at preventing the yen weakening further and hastening the need for higher Japanese interest rates. Growing speculation about a rise in Japanese rates, nevertheless, has reinforced the yen recovery, said analysts.

The Bank of Japan declined to comment on an overnight news agency report that it was not concerned about the pace of the dollar's recent retreat. The report was enough to keep a lid on a mild dollar recovery following a bout of short-covering in Tokyo.

"I think the market has now accepted that the official comfort zone for dollar/yen is closer to 115 than 125 and the interest rate story is being held up as a threat to counter any renewed slide in the yen," said a trader at a UK fund manager.
Japanese vice Finance Minister Takatoshi Kato said the economic recovery was intact and private demand was rising.

Analysts said the dollar/Europe story is very different. All official statements from European governments and central bank officials show satisfaction with the dollar/mark at current levels and there is little or no pressure for higher European interest rates.
The quarter-point cut in the Bank of Spain's key repurchase rate to 5.25 percent today underlines the easier monetary policy stance around the continent.
The drive to meet strict budgetary targets for European monetary union is forcing European authorities to keep a tight rein on fiscal policy and not monetary policy.

"The latest German budget news shows German may well miss the EMU entry criteria but the political statements indicate they will start EMU anyway," said Knuthsen at First Chicago. "This is raising speculation of a broad-based start to the single currency and that the euro will be a softer unit."

German finance minister Theo Waigel said he believes Germany will still meet the EMU budget criteria but he said he cannot rule out further tax rises. He said Bonn is counting on stepped-up privatisations to offset the estimated tax shortfall.

The ongoing speculation about the Fed's next move, meantime, will focus later today on the release of April housing starts and the May consumer sentiment index from the University of Michigan. However, analysts said these are relatively minor data releases and are unlikely to alter market expectations about the outcome of Tuesday's FOMC.
